episode_title: Nationalism Is Bad for the Nation

stories.topic: The India-Pakistan Cricket Match That Triggered the Episode
stories.summary: Amit was scrolling Twitter the day after a recent India-Pakistan tournament match. Indian players had refused to shake hands, captains and politicians produced 'belligerent noise' in press conferences, and social media exploded with virulence after the win. He found it doubly disturbing because India had a far superior team and won, and because historically Indian and Pakistani cricketers (Wasim Akram, Waqar Younis, Ramiz Raja) have been deeply popular and friendly across the border. The aggression came not just from politicians but from players themselves, against a people whose interests are nothing like the Pakistani military-jihadi state's.
stories.insight: Doug Stanhope's diagnosis of nationalism — 'hating people you have never met and taking pride in accomplishments you had nothing to do with' — was vivid in real time. The episode exists because a sporting moment exposed how readily a whole country can be roused to confuse the people of Pakistan with the Pakistani state.

stories.topic: Neeraj Chopra's Mother on Arshad Nadeem: 'Hamara Beta'
stories.summary: Neeraj Chopra had long mentored the Pakistani javelin thrower Arshad Nadeem, almost like an older brother despite being roughly the same age. At the most recent Olympics, Arshad won gold with an outlier 92-something throw and Neeraj didn't. A TV crew went to Neeraj's mother and asked what she felt; she replied, 'Arshad bhi tu hamara beta' — Arshad too is our son.
stories.insight: The right baseline for cross-border feeling, sitting alongside the cricket team's rancour as a counter-image. Genuine sportspeople recognise what their opponents have come through; the antidote to nationalist mob-rhetoric is the personal voice of someone who actually knows the other side.

stories.topic: How Gandhi Took Over the Congress via the Khilafat Alliance
stories.summary: Gandhi returned from South Africa around 1915. Gokhale told him not to do active politics for a year — just travel India — and then died a month later. Gandhi kept the promise, walking barefoot in tribute. By 1917-18 he was unknown at Congress gatherings. His real breakthrough came when he allied with the Ali brothers and their Khilafat movement (which wanted to revive the caliphate abolished after WWI). Gandhi was calling for Indian independence, the Ali brothers for the global Muslim ummah — logically incoherent partners. But the alliance was a tactical masterstroke that let Gandhi take over the Congress around 1920-21. Mohammad Ali Jinnah, then the last great moderate and presumed heir, couldn't decode the move; embittered, he turned, embraced the Muslim-nation cause, and the rest is history.
stories.insight: Two huge subcontinental nationalisms — Gandhi's Indian-independence movement and Jinnah's Pakistan project — were shaped by an opportunistic alliance with no coherent first principles. The accidents of history (a barefoot tour, a dead mentor, a tactical pact) carve the boundaries we now treat as eternal.

stories.topic: Marks for Shudh Hindi Because Nobody Speaks It
stories.summary: Amit got higher marks in Hindi than in English in both 10th and 12th standard, partly because he was 'lazy as fuck and didn't really study anything.' His hack: learn Shudh Hindi words and string them together — saying dwar instead of darvaza, mitron instead of dost. Even the teacher would just say 'give this motherfucker marks' because nobody actually speaks that constructed register.
stories.insight: A small autobiographical illustration of his bigger argument about Hindi/Urdu: the artificially purified vocabulary is a political artefact, not the lived language. The exam system itself rewarded the politically-constructed Sanskritised version over the living Hindustani people actually speak.

stories.topic: The Kashmiri Pandit Friend Who Banned His Sister's Salwar Kameez
stories.summary: A close former friend of Amit's, a Kashmiri Pandit, once told him he didn't let his sister wear salwar kameez because he viewed it as 'something Muslims wear.' In the 70s and 80s when Amit grew up, salwar kameez on women was widely seen as Muslim dress; today it has been completely normalised. Kurta on a man was once read as Eid-wear or a marker of being Muslim.
stories.insight: Clothes have no religion, but in the grip of nationalism they get assigned one — sometimes by people inside one's own family. A small, close-up demonstration of how the homogenising imagination of a nation polices everyday life, and how those policings can also reverse within a generation.

stories.topic: ICICI Bank — Whose Indian Company Is It Anyway?
stories.summary: When economic nationalists protect 'Indian' firms, what does the word even mean? ICICI Bank has roughly 90% foreign shareholding; in any reasonable world the entire top-management team would be foreign. Infosys has mostly foreign shareholders and mostly foreign customers. Yet the rhetoric of economic nationalism keeps treating these as units of Indian-ness whose competitive failures should be cushioned by the coercive power of the state.
stories.insight: The 'Indian company' is itself an imagined community in disguise. Once you actually trace the cap table and customer base, the protectionist case dissolves — and what's left is the universal pattern: politically-connected firms 'crying mummy' for the state to shield them from real competition.

stories.topic: Indian Data Centres Make No Engineering Sense
stories.summary: The Indian state pushes for 'data localisation' — data on Indian soil — under the rhetoric of sovereignty. Ajay walks through why this is engineering nonsense: in India's heat you pay more for AC; on India's intermittent grid you pay more for 24/7 electricity; the labour market for top-end data-centre engineers is thinner; tariffs raise the cost of imported equipment. The right answer is to put data centres in Greenland (cold air, abundant renewables) and have Indian users rent compute from there. The 'data is the new crude oil' framing dresses up a protectionist favour to certain Indian firms as national strategic interest.
stories.insight: Most 'sovereignty' arguments in tech economics are protectionist transfers wearing a flag. The narrow real exception is genuine defense-industrial security, and even there the right answer is foreign-policy diversification (e.g. closer ties with countries like Ukraine for components) rather than autarkic self-reliance.

recommendations.creator: Benedict Anderson
recommendations.context: Anderson's classic on nationalism, defining a nation as 'an imagined political community.'
recommendations.reason: Amit's favourite book on the subject and the spine of the episode. Source of the episode's central definition, the three paradoxes (modernity vs antiquity, universal vs particular, political force vs philosophical nebulousness), and the insistence that nations must be both 'limited' and 'sovereign' to make sense as a concept.

recommendations.creator: W. E. H. Lecky
recommendations.context: Lecky's late-19th-century work that introduces the idea of the 'expanding circle' of moral consideration.
recommendations.reason: Frames the optimistic arc of moral history — the circle of those we consider worthy of moral concern starts at family/kin and expands through tribe, village, nation, and ideally beyond. Useful as a reference point against which nationalism is measured: nationalism freezes the circle at one specific stage rather than letting it keep expanding.

recommendations.creator: Peter Singer
recommendations.context: Singer's book extending Lecky's frame, arguing the circle should one day include animals.
recommendations.reason: Cited as the natural extension of Lecky — Singer hopes the moral circle will reach animals. Amit's wry counterpoint: 'Alas, it hasn't even expanded to include all human beings,' which is exactly what nationalism prevents.

recommendations.item: The Ferment of Our Founders (Episode 272, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Shruti Kapila
recommendations.context: Amit's deep-dive episode with Shruti Kapila on Indian political thought.
recommendations.reason: Source of one of the episode's sharpest lines — Kapila's description of Hindutva as 'a theory of violence in search of a history.' Used to frame how all nationalisms feel forced to invent or rewrite a glorious past.

recommendations.creator: Manu Pillai
recommendations.context: Pillai's history of how Hindu identity was politically consolidated under colonial pressure.
recommendations.reason: Documents how, in pre-colonial India, Vaishnavites fought Shaivites more than they fought Muslims, and how a pan-Hindu sense of self emerged only later — first in opposition to Islam, then to British colonialism. Foundational for the episode's argument that 'Hindu' as a homogenous national category is a relatively recent construction.

recommendations.creator: Rabindranath Tagore and Mohandas Gandhi
recommendations.context: The collected letters between Tagore and Gandhi.
recommendations.reason: The primary source for Tagore vs Gandhi on nationalism. Gandhi was a 'soft nationalist' arguing for it as a tool of liberation; Tagore was where Amit and Ajay are today — that nationalism is simply toxic, full stop.

recommendations.creator: Rabindranath Tagore
recommendations.context: Tagore's collection of his three 1917 lectures on nationalism.
recommendations.reason: Direct source of the episode's most quoted passages — 'a cruel epidemic of evil eating into humanity's moral vitality,' 'the spirit of conflict and conquest is at the origin of Western nationalism,' 'nation is the greatest evil for the earth.' Amit calls Tagore prescient by a full century.

recommendations.creator: Francis Fukuyama
recommendations.context: Fukuyama's famous 1989 essay (with the question mark).
recommendations.reason: Invoked as the moment when, briefly, it seemed nationalism's grip might be loosening — a hope that has since been reversed. Amit notes the original title's question mark as historically important; Fukuyama himself was hedging.

recommendations.item: Gita Press and the Making of Hindu India
recommendations.creator: Akshaya Mukul
recommendations.context: Mukul's history of the Gita Press as an engine of Hindu nationalist consciousness.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it a masterpiece. Central to his argument that the secular tolerant 'idea of India' was imposed top-down by westernised elites while a different worldview was being cultivated bottom-up via vehicles like the Gita Press — which is why the secular project ultimately failed to hold.

recommendations.item: The Gita Press and Hindu Nationalism (Episode 139, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Akshaya Mukul
recommendations.context: Amit's long conversation with Akshaya Mukul on the Gita Press.
recommendations.reason: The audio companion to Mukul's book — recommended for listeners who want the full case for how deeply nationalist religious narratives were embedded in Indian society long before politics caught up.

recommendations.creator: George Orwell
recommendations.context: Orwell's classic essay describing serious sport as 'war minus the shooting.'
recommendations.reason: Source of the framing for the cricket-match outrage and the episode's broader critique of how nationalism poisons sport. Orwell's examples (a Glasgow vs Moscow football match, a Spanish football riot) prefigure exactly the dynamics India saw on its Twitter feeds after the Pakistan match.

recommendations.creator: Vaishnav Vyas
recommendations.context: The cinematographer of the show writes a football newsletter on Substack.
recommendations.reason: Amit and Vaishnav talk football constantly while shooting; the recommendation is offered as a window into a way of loving sport that is about playing philosophy ('what is Guardiola doing now?') rather than tribal allegiance to a national or club flag.

recommendations.item: The Life and Music of Shubha Mudgal (Episode 426, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Shubha Mudgal
recommendations.context: Amit's deep-dive episode with the Hindustani classical musician Shubha Mudgal.
recommendations.reason: Where Shubha-ji told Amit, surprisingly, that even Hindustani classical music is being touched by revisionist nationalism — including attempts at renaming ragas to scrub Muslim heritage. Cited as evidence that nationalist re-coding now reaches even art forms whose lineage is incontrovertibly multi-religious.

recommendations.item: In Service of the Republic: The Art and Science of Economic Policy
recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Kelkar and Shah's book on economic policy and the public-choice theory of the state.
recommendations.reason: Source of Ajay's framing of the principal-agent inversion: the state should be the agent of the people, but nationalism is the magic trick by which the state becomes the principal and the people become subjects. Background reading for the episode's chapter on how nationalism enables state oppression.

core_ideas.concept: A Nation Is an Imagined Political Community
core_ideas.explanation: Benedict Anderson's definition, which Amit treats as the spine of the entire episode. Unlike a prehistoric Dunbar-150 tribe whose members all actually knew one another, a nation is necessarily imagined: you have not met most of its members, you don't know their preferences, yet you imagine them as a homogenous 'we.' For Anderson the imagined community is also necessarily limited (no nation imagines itself coextensive with humanity) and necessarily sovereign (otherwise the concept collapses). Once you take the 'imagined' seriously, every nation becomes contingent rather than primordial.
core_ideas.quote: Nationalism is not the awakening of nations to self-consciousness. It invents nations where they do not exist. — Ernest Gellner

core_ideas.concept: Three Paradoxes at the Heart of Every Nation
core_ideas.explanation: Anderson's three paradoxes that Amit walks through. (1) Objective modernity vs subjective antiquity — nations are only a few centuries old, but every nation insists on a glorious ancient past, hence the constant invention of tradition (Hobsbawm). (2) Universal vs particular — every nationalism claims that having a nationality is universal to all humans, yet every actual nationalism is unique and often pits its particular against another's. (3) Political force vs philosophical nebulousness — nationalism has reshaped the world more than any ideology, but it has no canonical thinkers (no Locke, Smith, Marx of nationalism), only autocrats rationalising their own power.
core_ideas.quote: We are always certain about the present. It's the past that keeps changing. — Ajay Shah

core_ideas.concept: The Conditions That Birthed Modern Nationalism
core_ideas.explanation: Pre-1500 Europe had no nations — only kingdoms, empires, and intensely local feudal loyalties. Several converging shocks produced the nation: the War of the Roses weakened feudal overlords and made commoners and royals fight side by side, seeding 'English' consciousness; the rise of vernaculars (French, German) created new bases for shared identity; the printing press scaled narratives across distance; Locke and Rousseau introduced 'the will of the people' and popular sovereignty, which had to attach to some 'people'; and the Romantic Movement gave that people an emotional anchor in folk songs, fairy tales, and supposed ancestral glory. The American and French Revolutions fused these threads. By the late 19th century nationalism ruled the world.

Three pairs in which the same instinct produces opposite outcomes. (1) Liberation vs Oppression: nationalism rouses oppressed peoples to throw off colonial rulers, but it also gives every oppressor — Mussolini, Hitler — a free tool to label dissent 'anti-national.' (2) Cohesion vs Exclusion: a shared identity creates solidarity, but every 'we' immediately constructs a 'them' to be othered. (3) Cultural Pride vs Cultural Suppression: nationalism can revive Bengali, Irish, or African black culture, but it can equally be used to declare that Sufi music or Mughal cuisine is 'not ours.' Amit's verdict: in each pair the goods can be obtained by other means (liberalism, cities, cultural curiosity) while the bads are intrinsic to the nationalist frame.

Amit's deepest objection. To invoke a nation is to tie a person to an identity of birth or location and declare it the most important thing about them — bhakti sab hai bhar mein. Like every essentialising ideology (caste, race, religion), nationalism takes an accident of birth and makes it destiny: you are forever Indian, forever Hindu, forever a victim or oppressor. This denies the multitudes every individual contains. Walt Whitman's 'we contain multitudes' is the standing rebuke: each of us is many things, and any ideology that flattens us to one is an attack on our agency.
core_ideas.quote: We contain multitudes. — Walt Whitman, invoked throughout the episode

core_ideas.concept: The Magic Trick: How Nationalism Lets the State Become the Ruler
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's public-choice contribution. The right model of the state is principal-agent: the people are the principal, the state is their hired agent, fired and rehired when it underperforms. The pathology in many countries is the reverse — the state becomes the principal and the people become subjects. Nationalism is the conjuror's misdirection that enables the inversion. Once the rhetoric blurs 'Italy = the football team / the people / the state,' the state can claim that it is the nation, and any criticism becomes anti-national. This is the mechanism by which Mussolini ('It is not the people who make the state, but the state that makes the people'), Putin, and many others manufacture legitimacy for oppression.
core_ideas.quote: It is not the people who make the state, but the state that makes the people. — Benito Mussolini

core_ideas.concept: Top-Down Nationalisms All Fail in the End
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's reading of post-1947 India. Three nationalisms competed: a Hindutva nationalism (Savarkar), a Muslim nationalism that became Pakistan, and a secular tolerant 'idea of India' favoured by Nehruvian elites. The third won at the level of the constitution but was never built bottom-up — Akshaya Mukul's Gita Press shows how dramatically different the values flowing through Indian society actually were. Even Ambedkar called the constitution a 'mere topsoil.' Gandhi insisted change had to come bottom-up. A 'smug group of westernised elites' didn't take that seriously enough, and that is why a different kind of nationalism is back. All nationalisms are imposed by coercion; none arise naturally.

A working principle for cross-border feeling. There is the Pakistani state — what Pranay Kotasthane calls a 'military-jihadi complex' — whose legitimacy depends on framing India as a permanent enemy. Then there is the Pakistani people, whose interests are not aligned with that state at all and who are themselves oppressed by it. Treating those two as one is the elementary mistake of Indian nationalist rhetoric. Indians and Pakistanis are 'the same damn people' — same culture, same food, same music, same humour — separated mostly by which script their road signs use.

Hindustani — the Kichdi north Indian vernacular blending Persian, Arabic, Sanskrit, Prakrit and a dozen 'dialects' — was a beautiful spontaneous order. Then politics intervened: Urdu was painted Muslim, and a deliberately de-Persianised 'Hindi' (Shudh Hindi) was constructed and promoted. The literary canon of Hindi and Urdu writers were once interchangeable; the engineered cleavage between them is a political artefact. Schools still teach Shudh Hindi (dwar instead of darvaza, mitron instead of dost) — a register nobody actually speaks. The analogy: imagine Churchill saying 'we shall combat them in the boulevards' instead of 'we shall fight them in the streets.'
core_ideas.quote: A language is a dialect with an army.

core_ideas.concept: Sport, Tribe, and the Soccer War
core_ideas.explanation: Sport is structurally tribal, which is why nationalism colonises it so easily. Orwell's 'war minus the shooting' captured it; the 1969 Honduras-El Salvador qualifier escalated into a literal 100-day Soccer War with around 6,000 dead. Soccer didn't cause it — nationalism did, with sport as the trigger. Amit's escape route is to support clubs and players for their playing philosophy (Guardiola, his evolution, the thinkers of the game) rather than for their flag — and Ajay's tongue-in-cheek extension is that even national teams should be reformed as randomly-imagined communities with capitalist player markets, decoupling sport from nation entirely.

Every transaction is a positive-sum 'double thank you' moment. Lines on maps make no economic sense; whether you buy from Pune or Poland, both sides are better off. Tariffs and protectionism aren't punishments on foreigners — they're taxes on your own consumers. The protected firm gets to underperform; the consumer pays more for less. The whole 'self-reliance' rhetoric — including data localisation — is special pleading by politically-connected firms wrapped in the language of sovereignty. The narrow legitimate exception is defense-industrial security, and even there foreign-policy diversification beats domestic autarky.

core_ideas.concept: Nationalism Diminishes Us in Three Ways
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's closing argument is consequentialist, not first-principle. Nationalism diminishes us economically (protectionism makes us poorer), culturally (homogenising what should be a many-rivered ocean — Indic values shouldn't crowd out Enlightenment values; we should build cocktails of beliefs from everywhere), and in character (we lose access to the richness of the world's people, music, languages when we sort them into 'mine' and 'foreign'). Nationalism is a great diminishment of the self.
core_ideas.quote: I want the winds from the seven continents to blow through my nation. — Rabindranath Tagore

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's closing thought experiment. What if, when Unix and the internet were being built, Americans had branded them America-net or Unix-USA? Would the rest of the world have adopted them with the same enthusiasm? The whole 'global commons' character of those technologies — the willingness of every country to absorb them — depended on their not wearing a national flag. Nationalism in technology and standards would have made everyone, including Americans, poorer. A live argument against branding India's stack as 'Indian' before it has earned the world's adoption.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit imagining Tagore with YouTube: 'Imagine if this technology existed then. He could have done a YouTube show every week. And I think he would have called it Everything Is Everything. Shob kichu shob kichu.'
Amit on his Hindi exam hack: write nothing but Shudh Hindi (dwar, mitron) and 'even the teacher would say, just give this motherfucker marks. Because nobody speaks in Shudh Hindi.'

Ajay's modest reform proposal: 'We should form teams based on purely random imagined communities, put a little bit of old fashioned capitalism into it, have buying and selling of players. And you're done. You've decoupled it from the nation.'

Amit on biryani-as-anti-national rhetoric: 'Biryani is not anti-national. It is somewhat unhealthy, I agree, but it is deeply, deeply tasty, especially when made well. I am never going to give up biryani.'

Amit's deflationary line about Manchester United loyalty in India: psychologists say you tend to support whichever team is winning when you're 12-13, 'which is why there are chutias my age supporting Manchester United. Well, good luck, brother.'
Ajay on data centres: the right answer is to put them in Greenland and rent the compute back. 'Why do we get stuck on where the data sits? The fancy way is nationalism.'
Ajay's GK correction: 'Blue jeans did not originate in California. They originated in France — Denim, de Nimes, the region of Nimes.' Amit: 'GK GK.'
Doug Stanhope's definition of nationalism — 'hating people you have never met and taking pride in accomplishments you had nothing to do with.' Used as the moral hammer of the whole episode.
George Orwell's 'The Sporting Spirit' — sport as 'war minus the shooting,' invoked to frame the India-Pakistan cricket match outrage.
Ernest Gellner: 'Nationalism is not the awakening of nations to self-consciousness. It invents nations where they do not exist.'
Eric Hobsbawm's 'invention of tradition' — every nation, when invoked, finds itself forced to fabricate a golden age and a coherent past.
Carl Schmitt: 'politics needs an enemy.' Quoted to explain why nationalism is so convenient for the political — it auto-supplies an enemy in everyone outside the imagined community.

Mussolini: 'It is not the people who make the state, but the state that makes the people' — and 'Fascism stresses the importance of the state and accepts the individual only insofar as his interests coincide with those of the state.' The clearest statement of the magic trick.
Hitler's Lebensraum — Germany's nationalist case for territorial expansion, used to illustrate that imperial expansion is itself a form of nationalism.
Pranay Kotasthane's framing of the Pakistani state as a 'military-jihadi complex' — invoked to distinguish the Pakistani state from the Pakistani people.

Ambedkar's description of the constitution as a 'mere topsoil' — used by Amit to argue that any imposed-from-the-top nationalism (including secular Nehruvian nationalism) was bound to be brittle if not built bottom-up.
Walt Whitman: 'We contain multitudes' — Amit's standing rebuttal to every essentialising claim.
Bob Dylan, 'It's Alright, Ma (I'm Only Bleeding)': 'Even the president of the United States must some day stand naked.' Invoked when Amit argues clothes have no religion.

Tagore: 'a cruel epidemic of evil eating into humanity's moral vitality'; 'the spirit of conflict and conquest is at the origin of Western nationalism'; 'the nation, with its flags and pious hymns, cannot hide the fact that nation is the greatest evil for the earth.' The episode's prosecutorial chorus.
Tagore famously returning his Nobel Prize in protest — invoked to underline that he opposed nationalism even while supporting Indian independence.
Francis Fukuyama's 'The End of History?' — note the question mark; Amit insists Fukuyama himself was hedging the apparent triumph of liberalism.

Alexander Dugin as Putin's 'spiritual guide' — Ajay's grim hypothetical: 'If only Vladimir Putin could sign on for Rabindranath Tagore as his spiritual guide instead of Alexander Dugin, then millions of Russians would be alive today.'
The Soccer War (1969) — Honduras vs El Salvador football qualifier whose nationalism-charged riots escalated into a 100-day war with about 6,000 dead. Sport as trigger, nationalism as cause.

Robert Lucas / Berlin 1936 / Stalin's celebration of Pushkin in 1930 as the chief Soviet poet — the recurring pattern of nationalisms (even ostensibly internationalist communist ones) elevating one language and one canon over others.
